title: Adding a column
prompt:
The diastolic pressures were recorded too: 88, 76, 82, 84 and 94, in the
same order as the patients appear in the data frame.

Assigning to a column that doesn't exist yet creates it. Add them as a
column called `dbp`.
hint:
One value per patient, combined into a vector — then stored under the new
column's name.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.why:
`patients$dbp` didn't exist, so storing something there creates it — a
fifth column, lined up with the other four. The values are in the same
order as the patients appear in the data frame, so each one lands in
the right row.

checks.on_fail: `patients$dbp` should hold the five diastolic pressures, in order.

misconceptions.feedback:
There are five patients, so the column needs five values — one for
each patient, in the order they appear in the data frame. R won't
guess which patient a missing value belongs to.

There's no `dbp` column — check the capitals. `patients$DBP` would
create a *different* column, and asking for `patients$dbp` afterwards
quietly gives back nothing. Column names are exact.

title: Not enough values
prompt:
Only three diastolic pressures were written down. What happens?

```r
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82)
```
hint:
There are five patients. Which two would be missing a value — the last
two, or some other two?
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: An error — three values for five patients
options.feedback:
Right — the same rule as building a data frame in module 7. Every
column needs one value per patient, and R won't guess which patients
the three belong to.

There's one exception worth knowing: a *single* value is copied into
every row. `patients$ward <- "cardiology"` gives all five patients the
same ward. One value can't be ambiguous; three can.

That would mean R assuming the missing readings belong to the last two
patients. It won't. For all it knows, patient 2's is the one missing.

If you give R a single value to store as a column, it fills the whole
column with that value. But stretching three values across five
patients would pair readings with the wrong people, so it stops you
instead.

title: MAP for every patient
prompt:
In module 2 you worked out one patient's mean arterial pressure by hand.
Now do it for everyone at once.

MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3

Add it as a column called `map`. In R, multiply with `*` rather than ×.
hint:
Arithmetic on a column happens to every value at once, just as it did on a
vector. Use the two columns in the formula.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)

solution.why:
One line, five MAPs. R works down the rows in step: the first
patient's systolic with the first patient's diastolic, and so on. That
lining-up is what makes a data frame more than separate vectors.

Look at patient 3, though. Their systolic is missing, so their MAP is
`NA` too.

checks.on_fail:
The MAPs aren't right yet. Check the formula against the one above —
which pressure is doubled, and what the division applies to.
Patient 3's MAP should be `NA`, since their systolic is missing.

misconceptions.feedback:
That's the simple average of systolic and diastolic — the exact
mistake from module 2. Diastolic counts twice, because the heart
spends about two-thirds of each beat in diastole.

You've doubled the systolic instead of the diastolic. It's the lower
number that counts twice.

The division is only reaching part of the formula. Wrap the whole of
`patients$sbp + 2 * patients$dbp` in brackets before dividing by 3.

`sbp` and `dbp` only exist as columns inside `patients`. Write
`patients$sbp` and `patients$dbp` so R knows where to find them.

title: Look before you trust it
prompt:
Before trusting a new column, it's worth seeing it beside the columns it
was made from. Which of these shows `sbp`, `dbp` and `map` side by side,
for every patient?
hint: You're choosing columns, so the names go after the comma.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
patients$map <- (patients$sbp + 2 * patients$dbp) / 3

options.feedback:
Right — every row, three columns. Checking a new column against its
ingredients is the fastest way to catch a formula that's quietly
wrong. It's the same habit as checking the middle step in module 6.

That puts the names on the *row* side, asking for rows called "sbp",
"dbp" and "map". There aren't any, so you get three rows of `NA`s — and
no error.

Useful, but it summarises each column separately. You couldn't check
that one patient's MAP matches their own two pressures.

`$` takes one column at a time. `patients$sbp` is a vector, and a
vector has no columns to reach into.

title: What the new column inherited
prompt:
You run:

```r
summary(patients$map)
```

What will its `NA's` count be?
hint: MAP is made from two columns. Only one of them needs a missing value.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
patients$map <- (patients$sbp + 2 * patients$dbp) / 3

options.feedback:
Right. Patient 3's systolic is missing, so their MAP can't be worked
out, whatever their diastolic is. A new column inherits every missing
value from the columns it was made from.

So whenever you build a column from others, expect it to be missing a
value wherever any of its ingredients is.

It's new, but it was made from `sbp`, and patient 3's systolic is
missing. Anything calculated from a missing value is missing, so their
MAP is `NA`.

Only one patient is missing a systolic. The other four MAPs are
worked out normally — the missing value only affects its own row.

title: Changing a column in place
prompt:
Round the MAPs to one decimal place, storing the result back into the
same column.
hint: `round()` takes the value first, then the number of decimal places.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
patients$map <- (patients$sbp + 2 * patients$dbp) / 3

solution.why:
Storing into a column that already exists replaces it — the unrounded
values are gone, with no warning, the way reassignment always works.
That's fine here. Just be sure it's what you meant, because nothing
will stop you overwriting a column you needed.

checks.on_fail: The MAP column isn't rounded to one decimal place yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
The arguments are the wrong way round. `round(1, patients$map)` asks
to round the number 1 to a very large number of decimal places —
which is still 1. Value first, then places, or name them:
`round(patients$map, digits = 1)`.

title: The same column, with brackets
prompt:
Generated code often uses square brackets instead of `$`. Which of these
does the same as `patients$map <- (patients$sbp + 2 * patients$dbp) / 3`?
hint: A column name goes after the comma.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)

options.feedback:
Right. Blank before the comma for every row, `"map"` after it for the
column. It's the same as `patients$map`, and you'll see both.

This one fails silently, and it's worth knowing why. It puts `"map"`
on the *row* side, so R adds a new row called "map" and spreads the
five values across it — a sixth "patient" made of MAPs. No error, and
no new column.

Without quotes, R looks for a variable called `map`, and there isn't
one — so it stops with an error. Column names in square brackets need
quotes.

title: A column of TRUE and FALSE
prompt:
Add a column called `hypertensive` that is TRUE for every patient whose
systolic is 140 or more. In R, *greater than or equal to* is written
`>=`.
hint:
A comparison gives one TRUE or FALSE per patient. Store it the same way
you stored `dbp`.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
patients$map <- (patients$sbp + 2 * patients$dbp) / 3

solution.why:
The comparison asks each patient *is your systolic 140 or more?*, and
the answers become a column. Patient 3 gets `NA` — nobody can say
whether a missing reading is over 140.

checks.on_fail: `hypertensive` should be TRUE for the patients at 142 and 156.
Patient 3 should be `NA`, since their systolic is missing.

misconceptions.feedback: `sbp` only exists as a column inside `patients`. Write `patients$sbp`.

The comparison worked, but it wasn't stored anywhere, so there's no
`hypertensive` column. Put `patients$hypertensive <-` in front of it.

title: What fraction are hypertensive?
prompt:
Of the patients who have a systolic recorded, what fraction are
hypertensive?
hint:
In module 5, one function gave the *fraction* of TRUEs rather than the
count. And there's a missing value in this column.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
patients$dbp <- c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
patients$map <- (patients$sbp + 2 * patients$dbp) / 3
patients$hypertensive <- patients$sbp >= 140

solution.why:
Each TRUE counts as 1 and each FALSE as 0, so the average of a TRUE/FALSE
column is the fraction that are TRUE. With `na.rm = TRUE`, the patient
without a reading is left out — two hypertensive out of four measured.

checks.on_fail:
Not 0.5 yet. You want the fraction of the *measured* patients who are
TRUE.

misconceptions.feedback:
`NA` — the patient without a reading is still included. Add
`na.rm = TRUE`.

That's how many are hypertensive — a count. The question asks for the
fraction. One function gives the fraction of TRUEs directly.

That's 2 out of 5 — it counts the patient without a reading as *not*
hypertensive. `nrow(patients)` is 5, but only four patients were
measured. Nobody knows whether patient 3 is hypertensive, so they
shouldn't be in either count.

title: Labels the wrong way round
prompt:
`ifelse()` gives one of two values depending on a question. Its usage
line, also in the **Functions** panel, is:

```
ifelse(test, yes, no)
```

`test` is a comparison that gives TRUE or FALSE. `yes` is what you get
back when the answer is TRUE, and `no` is what you get back when it's
FALSE.

You were handed this to label each patient by age:

```r
patients$age_group <- ifelse(patients$age >= 65, "under 65", "65 and over")
```

What does the 67-year-old's `age_group` say?
hint:
For the 67-year-old, the test is TRUE. Which argument does `ifelse()` hand
back when the test is TRUE?
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.feedback:
Right — and every label in the column is backwards. The test is TRUE
for the 67-year-old, so `ifelse()` gives the second argument, `yes`,
which here is `"under 65"`. The labels were typed in the wrong order.

It runs cleanly and every value looks sensible. Nothing but reading
the call against its usage line catches it.

That's what the code was *meant* to say. But `ifelse()` hands back its
second argument when the test is TRUE, and the second argument here
is `"under 65"`.

It runs without complaint. Both labels are valid text, so R has no way
to know they're in the wrong places.

title: Labels the right way round
prompt:
Write it correctly. Name each argument — `test`, `yes` and `no` — so the
order can't go wrong.
hint:
`test = ` the question, `yes = ` the label when it's TRUE, `no = ` the
label when it's FALSE.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

solution.code: patients$age_group <- ifelse(test = patients$age >= 65, yes = "65 and over", no = "under 65")
solution.why:
With the names written in, anyone reading the line can check each label
against its condition — and the order stops mattering, because R
matches them by name. That's exactly the protection the last exercise
needed.

checks.on_fail:
The labels aren't right yet. The 67- and 71-year-olds should be
"65 and over".

misconceptions.feedback:
Inside a call, attach a value to an argument with `=`, not `<-`. `<-`
stores something in a variable; `=` says *this value is for that
argument*.

That gives the right labels — but only because you typed them in the
right order this time. The last exercise shows how easily that goes
wrong. Write `test =`, `yes =` and `no =` in front of each one, so the
labels can't end up backwards.

match.expr: identical(tolower(patients$age_group), c("65 and over", "under 65", "65 and over", "under 65", "under 65")) && !identical(patients$age_group, c("65 and over", "under 65", "65 and over", "under 65", "under 65"))

misconceptions.feedback:
The labels are in the right places, but typed with different capital
letters from the prompt. To R, `"65 And over"` and `"65 and over"` are
different labels — so a later filter looking for one would never find
the other. Match them exactly.

Still backwards. `yes` is the label for when the test is TRUE — for
patients who *are* 65 and over.

title: A column on a copy
prompt:
```r
older <- patients[patients$age >= 65, ]
older$flag <- TRUE
```

Does `patients` now have a `flag` column?
hint: Think back to what filtering does to the original.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: No — `older` is a separate data frame
options.feedback:
Right. Filtering handed you a new data frame, stored as `older`, and
adding a column changes only `older`. `patients` is exactly as it was.

The flip side is worth knowing: if you meant to flag those patients in
the original, this code quietly does nothing to it.

`older` was made *from* `patients`, but it's a copy. Changing it
doesn't reach back into the original.

options.text: Yes, but only for the rows aged 65 and over
options.feedback:
That's what someone often *wants* here, but it isn't what happens.
`older` is a separate copy, so `patients` gets no new column at all.

title: Filling in the missing reading
prompt:
Someone wanted to record *why* patient 3's systolic is missing, so they
wrote a note into the cell:

```r
patients$sbp[3] <- "not taken"
```

What type is the `sbp` column now?
hint: A column is a vector, and a vector holds one type.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

options.text: Character — the whole column is text now
options.feedback:
Right. One text value turned every value in the column into text —
`142` is now `"142"`. In a spreadsheet-style view it looks exactly the
same as before.

Why it matters: try to do any math on that column and it won't work,
because every value in it is now character, not numeric.

The instinct was a good one: *why* a value is missing is worth
recording. It just belongs in its own column, like
`patients$sbp_note`, so the numbers stay numbers.

options.text: Still numeric — only one cell changed
options.feedback:
A column can't be mostly numbers with one note in it. It's a vector,
and a vector holds one type, so the whole column became text.

options.text: Mixed — numbers with one piece of text
options.feedback:
That's how it would look in a spreadsheet, and exactly why it's easy to
miss. R doesn't allow mixed columns: one piece of text makes every
value text.
